title: Devolution is not the only answer – higher education still needs a national policy agenda
summary: New PM Andy Burnham wants to go further and faster on devolution, but for higher education, local focus still needs to be underpinned with a national policy infrastructure. David Kernohan assesses the options for action
full_text:
Andy Burnham is passionate about localism and devolution.

We should, however, be wary of anticipating policymaking that sees everything through that lens – there are many areas of government activity that require policy and implementation at a national level. While aspects of everything can – and arguably should be – devolved, there is much that cannot be. And higher education is a great example.

The story begins

Changing the Prime Minister, and tweaking the cabinet, may improve the “vibes” of government. Certainly it will make a difference to the quality and relatability of public communication at a senior level. It is emphatically not going to transform the economy over the summer – the latest rumours about Shabana Mahmood as chancellor emphasise just how much the financial sector craves continuity and orthodoxy within a very narrow boundary.

That said, his leadership acceptance speech reversed the Brexit arguments and claimed “the right gave away control.” If we read this as a commitment to making active choices rather than passively accepting the decisions made by the market, we assume not only a desire to pick winners (and become unpopular with those who are not chosen) but a need to have the data and evidence required to underpin radicalism and the courage to act on these conclusions.

If Ed Miliband’s net zero plans – plans that were themselves both Treasury orthodoxy and Conservative party policy in recent years, but are now routinely downplayed in an attempt to win the support of the so-called “hero voter” – are beyond the pale, we can probably rule out massive changes to policies around government borrowing or spending. Some variants of the existing fiscal rules will remain, and given existing commitments, the chances for new spending at anything other than a marginal level are limited.

Caught in a rat race, terminally

In the education portfolio, commitments to SEND reform and increases to teacher pay will almost certainly be honoured, and will form a big part of departmental discretionary spending. We should also expect a material response to the second (recommendation bearing) half of Alan Milburn’s review of support for young people not in education, employment, or training (NEET) as a signature Burnham policy. The response to the next phase (tentatively expected in the autumn) could well be the new administration’s first serious intervention in the skills debate.

This also chimes in well with Burnham’s experiences in Manchester – last weeks’ Greater Manchester post-16 pathways report doesn’t directly address the NEET issue, but aims for a more cohesive system that addresses the transition and guidance issues that can put learners off post-compulsory training. The tentative Milburn recommendations run along similar lines – if there is even a small amount of additional funding available for post-16 education this is where it will go. Anyone looking to arrange higher education lobbying activity should lean into this agenda.

I’m a professional cynic but my heart’s not in it

The lifelong learning entitlement (LLE) is – as we’ve been over on Wonkhe many times before – a potentially transformative policy hamstrung by questionable implementation decisions. Why, for instance, can you only access modules drawn from existing courses? – and if the answer to that is “to enable progression”, where is the national work on credit transfer? Why are eligible subject areas determined by priority industries rather than employer needs within those industries? How is LLE provision regulated for quality and academic standards?

Most glaringly of all, the LLE posits a world in which workers borrow from the government in order to fund their own development and training. The UK has historically been weak in employer-provided training – a facet of our culture that might well explain elements of the productivity puzzle.

It would be a straightforward win – for the economy and for learners – to re-examine some of these Johnson-era guardrails. The plans, and the associated uncapped spending commitment, which could contribute substantially to loan outlay and repayment debt, could achieve much better results with a bit more flexibility. And, frankly, a bit more promotion at a national level – it’s an agenda that calls for a minister to champion it. We could also raise the question of localism: why can’t the people who write local skills improvement plans have a say in what is in and out of bounds, based on local needs?

Whoever Burnham appoints to the Education or Skills brief, the LLE is the big plan currently in train. With a few tweaks it could offer better answers to some very current and very Burnham-esque concerns.

For the faint at heart, a brand-new start

The LLE, is – when we get down to it – an intervention aimed at spurring access to and participation in higher education. Although participation rates are rising – slowly – and both the number of applications and the number of offers made are the highest on record, there is a sense in which a message has been sent that university is not for everyone. There are concerns about shrinking rates of return (though it is not methodologically straightforward to tease out what is going on here), and a growing cultural sense that young people traveling for university study is antagonistic to local growth and development.

Burnham has expressed his take within the growing cross-party consensus that university should not be the “default” route. This policy direction should not be read as expressing a need to “deprioritise” higher education, after all a large and growing population of young people (and their parents) are deciding that university is the right route to support their aspirations and aptitudes.

But the data is clear. Working class and minoritised people are less likely to apply to university – a factor that has informed recent Office for Students work on access, which again is focused locally and designed to drive aspiration. It just needs a bit more focus, a bit more visibility, and a bit more accountability. And an increased focus on non-traditional routes.

Life’s a different story

The idea that the default university experience is three years of undergraduate study (as pervasive as it has been against decades of trumpeted innovations) often starts with the application process. However much we promote other routes into higher level study, the experience appears to be designed to funnel people towards what students have done for generations. It should be as easy to find and take an LLE module, a level 4 apprenticeship unit, a higher technical qualification, or anything else that may emerge as it currently is to find an undergraduate degree.

UCAS’s course finder is the principal means by which people find courses, and although recent changes have improved things it does still slant people towards the three-year default and the classic application cycle. And it still doesn’t integrate with the way people access student finance via Student Finance England. There are some cheap fixes that could happen here – with much better use made of the government’s own Discover Uni platform – or the (public) data on (publicly supported) courses could be opened up to allow for other means of discovery.

There is a similar articulation job to be done around advice and guidance – which again plays into the NEET discourse. The advice you are able to access on post-compulsory education and training depends on your background: the experiences of your family and friends, the focus of your school or college, and your own finances. There’s been various attempts to bring these various sources together, and Milburn looks set to recommend another go.

Paying the price of living life at the limit

Higher education has been on a crisis footing ever since the pandemic, and arguably for some years before that. While there have been some questionable (to say the least) policy decisions made during that time, a big part of the problem has been so much change and so little stability.

A case in point is on international recruitment. Long a key income stream for many providers, the rules (both in broad and very technical terms) have changed so often it has become impossible to think strategically about where and how to intervene. The fee levy is just the latest constraint to consider – what professionals at this end of the sector are primarily asking for is stability and reliability. It feels an easy win to leave stuff well alone, but sadly clampdowns on immigration are both cheap (in the short term) and popular.

Likewise, there are many options as to how best to assess the quality and standards of provision – after a decade in the wilderness we are gradually edging back towards some kind of cyclical review process via the redesign of the TEF. There’s still work to be done – notably, the outcomes measures don’t really work for modular study – before the final form is announced, but it would be really good to see an emphasis on predictability and stability rather than any further regulatory innovations. And even better to come up with a regimen that supports improvement rather than aims to catch out providers who don’t fit the standard model and expectations.

The final piece of the puzzle for the Burnham years may well be unleashing the power of collaboration both within and around higher education. Various rules around competition and tax prevent some of the very efficiencies that the post-16 education and skills white paper (whatever happened to it?) looks to identify and implement. If the government remains committed to collaboration, and for that matter the specialisation that would follow, it probably needs to tidy up some of that.

It’s a helping hand that makes you feel wonderfully bland

Like the rest of the country, the sector appears to hold the opinion that things might – if we are lucky – be a little bit better than under Starmer. Expectations, especially at the senior end, are very limited.

Burnham starts his premiership offering “Manchesterism” and good vibes. Neither of these things will address the many problems higher education currently faces, and anyone hoping otherwise will be disappointed. When our main ask is a special administration regime, and even that feels unlikely, it is an accurate indicator of the lack of bandwidth available to deal with the sector’s problems.

The strength arising from a change in prime minister is a change in the narrative. Burnham – an experienced political operator, is good at narrative – people genuinely seem to like him. And a track record of local delivery is encouraging. Higher education won’t be his priority – but maybe it can demonstrate how it can help him get to the things he really cares about.

title: Higher education would look very different if local areas were in control
summary: Michael Salmon has read 39 LSIPs so you don’t have to – but you should, as they reveal plenty about what places want from their universities
full_text:
Place-based collaboration will become the “new operating principle for UK PLC,” Andy Burnham promised in his People’s History Museum speech back at the end of June.

Beyond the airy sentiment, this was quickly followed by a proper policy commitment: all government departments and agencies would be required to support strategic and local authorities with staffing and resources. The mechanics of such a pledge will take some time to emerge, but we could be looking at the Office for Students, Skills England, UKRI, DfE and DSIT all obliged to – in some form – stump up personnel for work in individual local areas.

In this context, it’s worth thinking about what local-led priorities for higher education would look like if they had greater heft behind them. Conveniently, the latest round of Local Skills Improvement Plans for England have recently gone live.

LSIPs

The new version of LSIPs were launched last November, hot on the heels of the post-16 white paper. In a nutshell, each region of England (39 in total – now covering the whole nation and contiguous with local administrative geography) would have a plan for skills and technical education priorities and actions, drawn up collaboratively by employer representatives, local government, and education providers.

Importantly for higher education, there were greater expectations for HE institutions to have a role in governance and implementation, and for the plans to cover skills needs all the way up to level 8.

Drafts were submitted at the end of March – I’ve heard criticisms from some of those involved that the process was too rushed, but there’s clear evidence of wide-ranging engagement with employers and other local stakeholders. To pick a fairly representative example, the plan for Greater Devon was based on

1,405 direct employer interactions and 194 engagements with providers, statutory stakeholders and partners, alongside 42 events reaching over 3,000 businesses. Primary research was structured through four core instruments: the LSIP Employer Survey, the LSIP Telemarketing Survey targeting non-member SMEs, the 100 Voices Campaign, and the LSIP Workforce Skills Snapshot.

Especially in the new place-based context we supposedly find ourselves in, how these stakeholders (and by extension, these plans) speak about higher education – in particular, about higher-level qualifications and about university graduates – feels very relevant. If local areas are to receive more power, then how would they seek to wield it?

Though we should caveat at this point that the plans provide a necessarily partial understanding of what the local areas they seek to speak for actually require from their education systems. The process is designed around employer needs (and wants), mediated by the Skills and Post-16 Education Act framing as well as last autumn’s Skills England guidance and the quango’s supporting role in the process.

This “national steer” comes across very strongly. Most plans see action within local skills systems through the lens of national-level policies: the LLE, foundation apprenticeships, V levels, apprenticeship units. These are the changes which are happening, and therefore they frame the actions that each plan can commit to.

And as a window into the concerns that local government and employers share, the plans are pretty consistent. Almost all express worries about NEETs, about left-behind areas within their geographies, and about patchy apprenticeship take-up (including some thinly-veiled outrage about the defunding of level 7 and management standards). And all are preoccupied with how the proliferation of AI will change local employment.

Specialisation

In coming up with the new plans, local areas were instructed to give consideration to both the industrial strategy and the post-16 education and skills white paper. The former comes through very clearly – each plan chooses its priority areas, taken from the industrial strategy with a mix of local sectors of strength thrown in for good measure.

The plans’ agreed actions then focus on these sectors, outlining how the skills system can better support employment and employer training. There are often explicit commitments for further and higher education institutions to focus their activities on certain sectors – which to an extent is coherent with the white paper’s quest for greater specialisation. But it’s interesting to reflect that the white paper framed the specialisation agenda more in terms of research strengths informing teaching provision, and in higher education institutions being strategic about how they “consolidate”.

Within the LSIPs, there’s a completely different impetus: the plans’ starting point is the local industries that are most important, and then education and skills provision will follow in service to this. It is still a mechanism for specialisation – but there’s no link made to research, and it’s hard to gauge to what extent this could really ever be complementary.

Still, if you’re wondering how greater local power would play out in education and skills, this ought to give you something of an idea: provision shaped by key local industries, or at least greater exhortation for this to be the case.

Graduates

An illuminating recent article from Yorkshire Universities’ John Harrison reflecting on the LSIP development process made the case that graduates need to be at the heart of plans – not just fitting into the labour market, but shaping it.

It’s true that many of the new plans are deeply worried about graduate retention. Cheshire and Warrington’s says it is a “recurring theme across employer engagement.” Dorset’s notes that the area is “characterised by low graduate retention” and launches work with HE and FE providers to remedy this. Hampshire’s plan observes the competition with London for graduates.

Liverpool’s plan concludes that “graduate out-migration reflects a lack of clear, industry-aligned career pathways within the City Region.” Swindon and Wiltshire’s plan, which frequently bemoans the lack of a local university, suggests that “many young people leave the area to pursue higher education opportunities elsewhere and do not subsequently return.” The North East LSIP says that “the region struggles to attract and retain graduates who do not have prior roots in the area.”

And yet this isn’t consistent. Many of the newly published plans express no concerns about graduate outflow (Berks, Bucks, Essex, Lincolnshire, Norfolk and Suffolk – to name a few). While many local areas seem to be thinking deeply about how to ensure that graduates are well-deployed in local labour markets, and commissioning further research on the topic (the Cheshire and Warrington LSIP notes that the University of Chester will take the lead on this, for example), others have their priorities elsewhere.

On the level

The West Midlands LSIP has an entire page titled “increasing modularity.” It’s by no means an outlier – to the extent that the plans speak to changes they would like to see in university-level provision, the calls for modular, or flexible, or “bite-sized” training offers are pretty common.

Duration aside, there’s limited thinking within many of the plans about higher education-level study. It’s noted in some that Skills England’s research has suggested much future demand for skills and qualification will be at higher levels, but this doesn’t track through to the commitments that get made.

And it is really visible at level 7 and 8. This was supposed to be one of the big Labour innovations around LSIPs, which would cement universities’ role within the process and join local systems up with the industrial strategy. Yet such a join-up doesn’t seem to have stuck the landing.

With 39 different plans, it’s not the case that there are no mentions of postgraduate-level needs – but they are few and far between. Hampshire, Cumbria and Stoke are all thinking about level 8 needs, in specific sectors and with reference to longer-term competitiveness as opposed to immediate shortages. Buckinghamshire’s LSIP, on the other hand, abruptly states that “currently there are no skill needs at level 8,” though it promises to keep the matter under review.

It could be that expecting local governments and employers to plan out their labour force needs at the highest qualification levels is too complex a task in a short time-frame – and one that might particularly benefit from Burnham’s commitment to having national agencies provide dedicated resource to local projects. One of the LSIPs gestures at a commitment to “integrate early-stage R&D funding with technical training” and “connect the region’s technical education courses directly with Research England.” This sounds nice, but clearly would benefit from further unpacking.

Or it could be that there aren’t obvious levers for the plans to reach for at level 7 and level 8. If the government had policy in train in this area, or was communicating a vision for what it wanted, then the LSIPs would draw on this (in the same way that they lean into modular provision at lower levels, or more HE-FE collaboration). But it doesn’t, and so they don’t.

Universities’ role

There is plenty for universities in England to be thinking about here, both arising from their own region’s plan (which they will have been involved in) and the wider picture of what local areas want – or say they want – from higher education. Management training is a recurring refrain, for example, especially in SMEs.

Many of the plans present their local higher education institutions as active partners, responsible for the success of specific initiatives. University of Hertfordshire is conducting research into access to training, which will be fed back into the LSIP. In Liverpool, Edge Hill University is running an SME-focused AI diagnostic project. The North East LSIP assigns a lead university for each of its priority sectors, with a mandate to get the other higher education institutions in the area collaborating. In the West Yorkshire plan, the role of the Yorkshire Universities regional grouping in convening and enabling collaboration is prominent throughout.

My overall takeaway from reading the 39 plans over the course of this last week is that local area stakeholders (of the sort responsible for LSIPs) are proud of their higher education institutions, but see their immediate skills needs elsewhere and at lower levels. Many of the things that the sector likes to speak about the most – international students, economic contribution in gross value added – don’t really figure. And you’d be forgiven for thinking that many local areas wouldn’t see positive graduate destinations as anything to celebrate, unless this means those graduates who are staying in that region.

The LSIP aspiration of joining up local skills systems is gradually taking shape, though lack of funding, capacity and accountability all remain open questions, as I wrote when the new guidance arrived last year. A fundamental reshaping of the English state, as Andy Burnham is currently keen to promise, could address some of those challenges.

Perhaps a more persistent concern is that, if you structure education systems around the language of skills needs, employer instincts, and learners’ immediate outcomes, then you might indeed end up with a landscape which can be described as more responsive to local areas. But it can also read like an instrumentalist diminishing of what higher education at its best is really about, and which struggles to connect with universities’ roles in research and the creation of knowledge, as well as culture, citizenship, and much else. If local areas do receive more power, then the mechanisms to understand how best they can be served will need strengthening as well.

title: Beyond equity of regard to equity in practice for college and university-based higher education
summary: "Parity of esteem" for college and university-based HE comes from a shared quality architecture and governance framework, not vague policy aspirations, argue Nic Beech and Rebecca Parks
full_text:
Today, Andy Burnham enters 10 Downing Street, having been absolutely clear he wants a country with greater, and more evenly experienced, prosperity, and that he sees devolution as crucial to achieving that.

Making local economies better requires higher and further education working together – and working better with their local government. Regional mayors have a chance to do more with their local universities and colleges, rather than a central state doing things to them.

But the backdrop to these policy debates is a public discourse that increasingly pits the purpose and value of further education and higher education against each other, too often based on perceived value, a partial reading of the evidence, or a confused policy architecture which practically disincentivises collaboration even as it rhetorically demands it.

But the new PM’s own experiences in Greater Manchester highlights that different futures are possible. In Salford, where both our university and our college are based, we see the realities of an education and skills ecosystem across the city-region committed to deepening integration and delivering a joined-up system that enables learners to progress through FE directly into work or to HE, and then into gainful employment.

The City Council plays a key role in the governance of both the college group and the university, and the civic university agreement with the council and developing Salford Innovation Board mean that there is consistent discussion between education, the city, business and the public sector.

We see adult learners moving from work into courses in FE or HE to develop their skills before returning to the workplace as well as the traditional school-college-university pathway. University students act as tutors in our schools and staff and PhD researchers contribute to teaching in our colleges.

But, we also recognise the potential fragility of this ecosystem constrained by structural, regulatory, and financial pressures that can force institutions into positions of competition rather than collaboration. We share a sense of the possibilities but have also direct experience of the pitfalls.

First, that the perceived value of HE and FE is so different, despite evidence that this should not be so; and, second, that the internal cultures of FE and especially HE institutions can create barriers to collaboration.

The experiences of Greater Manchester and the maturity of its devolved system, offer a ready test-bed to grapple with exactly these sorts of questions and have illuminated a way forward.

Shared quality code

On perceived value, we must do more to communicate the high, internationally-recognised standards of UK education across FE and HE. Students, their parents and carers, as well as employers and the general population need easy access to well-founded evaluation of the impact of higher education across the tertiary sector – whether in college or university settings.

The UK Quality Code is a sector-owned code devised and agreed through the Quality Council for UK HE which does exactly this. It establishes a shared understanding of, and foundation for, how we deliver quality – and it is endorsed by representative bodies of universities, colleges, specialist and independent providers, as well as NUS, and across all four nations of the UK. It is genuinely owned by the sector, and each nation has its own mechanisms for quality enhancement or assurance implemented by the separate funder-regulators.

The Quality Code is evidence that a more integrated system is possible, premised on a shared understanding of quality provision – we have the mechanisms already to facilitate and drive greater shared understandings of quality in tertiary integration.

We also have potential models for delivery of that more integrated system. The recent Curriculum and Assessment Review for pre-18 education introduced V-levels. These new qualifications are about both equity and choice: equity in vocational qualifications being valued in the same way as academic ones, and choice in students being able to either specialise or combine academic and vocational qualifications.

System-wide approaches such as these are essential if we are to avoid framing FE and HE either in opposition or as entirely separate pathways leading to entirely different outcomes.

Shared learning and conversation across the Greater Manchester system also bringing in voices from the tertiary systems of Scotland and Wales, and other regulatory, policy, or education-based stakeholders in the UK, have helped us to develop an inclusive approach to quality operating for different parts of the sector and coordinating with professional bodies and regulators. This creates meaningful regional collaborations between all HE providers and local government, which can emphasise particular priorities or industrial/research-oriented specialities. Localities will also need the capacity to balance their own needs and wants with national and global trends in the demand for graduates.

FE and HE can cooperate in constructing pathways into and through technical, professional and traditional academic routes and onto employment, connecting across the education system and businesses and employing organisations. It is here where we can ensure diverse learners benefit from educational opportunity through great support and pedagogy.

Mutual regard

To tackle the second challenge, we have to be honest that within both FE and HE, the governance structures and regulation require our governing bodies to be focused on institutional success and survival. Too often, this can inadvertently militate against a systematic approach in which we might need to consider much greater mobility of students, staff and resources between institutions.

But there is so much to be gained from close engagement, as we have found in Greater Manchester. For example, HE can learn a lot from FE about navigating troubled financial times. The college system has already gone through very significant efficiencies and restructuring, establishing both “‘academic” and “vocational” routes with strong employer engagement and a professional approach to education; in the current straightened circumstances, HE will need to follow suit.

FE has also made significant advances in supporting mental health, educational and personal transitions, and adaptable curricula and pedagogies. There are clearly differences between FE and HE, most obviously in research, but where we are concerned with the success of learners, there is much that we need to learn about systemic solutions.

Greater collaboration with other institutions and local government does pose challenges – HE institutions are, rightly, jealous of their autonomy from government, because academic freedom to investigate and critique is a key pillar of a free society. FE colleagues too often find their expertise is not properly valued by their HE counterparts.

But if we are to achieve a sustainable post-16 education and skills system, we must overcome these barriers. For example, developing a shared statement of practice establishing structures and governance frameworks that enable genuine equity of regard, voice and outcome within and between providers and pathways. This will also require significant culture change, particularly within HE that acknowledges any innovation will only develop at the pace of trust.

There is also a need to better enable staff and student mobility within and between FE and HE. This too needs a quality framework specifically designed to enable mobility of learners and credits, and this may challenge us to not only care for our institutions but also commit to more integrated systems which could be facilitated by regional structures.

Keep pushing forward

We are not pretending to have oven-ready solutions to these challenges in Salford. Though we see a pathway towards a more integrated regional offer, and we feel we have some sense of the shape and nature of the changes required, we know this is a transformation that will not happen overnight. We know the pace of change will vary between regions, depending on the context of collaboration and of competition. And we know changes need to be balanced by students having choices to study locally for careers that could take them anywhere in the world.

But we intend to live the values of FE/HE collaboration, so to chart a way forward, we will be setting out a series of policy considerations for (regional) post-16 education and skills systems, published via the Quality Council.

We can only move forward if we confront challenges in existing policy and formalise regional governance structures with relevant representatives across regulators, education, policy and government, which empower and enable institutions to undertake the practical work of implementing the design principles that all the participants in GM’s tertiary system have developed.

A devolved and effective tertiary system is absolutely possible, but it will take care, conviction and courage to build it.

title: WEEKEND READING: Universities aren’t just graduate factories, they’re architects of opportunity
summary:
This blog was kindly authored by Professor Gillian Murray, Vice-Chancellor, University of Bradford. The post WEEKEND READING: Universities aren’t just graduate factories, they’re architects of opportunity appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Professor Gillian Murray, Vice-Chancellor, University of Bradford.

Increasingly, universities are judged not just by the quality of education they provide but by what happens after graduation. This is entirely understandable. Students want confidence that their degrees will lead to meaningful careers, while employers need graduates who are job-ready from day one and who can add value to their businesses. Governments, meanwhile, want to see education translated into productivity, prosperity and economic growth.

But the debate has become dominated by the question of how effectively universities prepare students for the jobs that already exist. Important though that is, it only addresses part of a much wider debate about the value universities create for individuals, employers and society.

My view, grounded in years of experience leading large-scale partnership programmes between universities, industry and government, is that we are looking at this the wrong way round. Universities have a distinctive and under-recognised role as convenors.

Across the UK, higher education institutions are already making profound contributions to their regions and to the national economy. They support entrepreneurs, help businesses innovate, commercialise research, develop new technologies and bring together partners to tackle complex societal challenges.

Yet we rarely talk about these contributions in a coherent way. Employability, research, enterprise, innovation and civic engagement are often treated as separate agendas. In reality, they are deeply interconnected. Together, they form a powerful system for generating opportunity.

Perhaps the greatest strength of a modern university is not simply that it teaches, carries out research and innovates. It is that it convenes. It acts as a conduit through which otherwise disparate partners can connect. No other institution brings together students, researchers, employers, entrepreneurs, investors, policymakers and communities in quite the same way. Universities are uniquely positioned to connect ideas with investment, talent with opportunity and research with real-world application.

This convening power is becoming increasingly important as the economy evolves. Artificial intelligence, demographic change, the transition to net zero and new patterns of work are reshaping labour markets at pace. In such an environment, no curriculum can ever fully keep up. Responding to employer demand will always matter, but it is no longer sufficient.

We must move beyond asking what skills are needed today and begin designing, together, the industries and opportunities of tomorrow. Doing this will require thinking across three horizons and not just focusing on the short term.

The first horizon is preparing students for today’s labour market through excellent education, placements, apprenticeships and close collaboration with employers. This remains fundamental to the mission of every university. It is precisely what we’re doing with Sovereign Health Care, a Bradford partnership that will help alleviate pressure on the NHS and give hundreds of students valuable hands-on experience.

The second horizon is co-designing tomorrow’s workforce. This means bringing together universities, businesses, colleges and government to anticipate emerging skills needs, identify future sectors and develop provision before shortages occur.

The third horizon is creating entirely new forms of opportunity. At Bradford, we are doing with this through our Bradford-Renduchintala Enterprise Ecosystem, which offers anyone (staff, students, members of the public) the chance to gain seed-funding, put business ideas in front of experts and investors, and take those ideas from concept to market. It is through research, innovation and entrepreneurship like this, universities help launch new companies, support the adoption of emerging technologies and attract investment into new areas of growth.

This third horizon, despite often being the least visible, may ultimately be the most transformative. It is here that universities contribute, not only to employment, but to productivity and economic renewal. This is where new industries emerge and where future jobs are created.

For many years, we have been comfortable describing universities in terms of separate missions, teaching, research, innovation, enterprise and civic engagement. The institutions that will flourish in the coming decade will be those that connect these strengths into a single, coherent purpose. That purpose is creating opportunity: for students to build meaningful careers, for businesses to innovate and grow, for researchers to see their work deliver tangible impact, for places to develop and prosper.

But if universities are to act as architects of opportunity, this requires a shift not only in what we do, but in how we think.

It also has clear implications for leadership. The role of a Vice-Chancellor is not only to safeguard academic excellence and institutional sustainability, but to act as a convenor, bringing together partners around shared ambitions and enabling collaboration at scale.

Universities have always brought together people, ideas and possibilities. What has changed is the urgency and the expectation that this results in tangible impact beyond our campuses.

To do this, we need to connect the capabilities we already have more effectively, align them more strategically and articulate their contribution more clearly.

If we can do that, we will move beyond the prevailing narrative that the principal role of universities is to prepare graduates for existing jobs and instead we can begin to help shape the economy those graduates will inherit. In doing so, universities will fulfil one of their most important roles: not simply responding to opportunity but creating it.

title: S&P: Despite enrollment gains, margins have worsened at colleges
summary: The credit ratings agency found increases in median headcounts across colleges it rates, but also weakening operating margins in fiscal 2025.
full_text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

Dive Snapshot:

Despite enrollment growth at public and private colleges in fiscal 2025, both sectors saw their operating margins worsen, according to reports released this week by S&P Global Ratings.

Public colleges’ 2.1% median enrollment growth of full-time-equivalent studentsoutpaced the 0.7% increase at private colleges in fiscal 2025 across S&P’s portfolio of rated institutions

The median operating margin across S&P’s 286 rated private institutions in fiscal 2025 was -0.4%,down from -0.3% the prior year. Public colleges showed healthier performances with a median operating margin of 0.7% across S&P’s 145 rated institutions in the sector, but that was still down slightly from 0.9% the prior year.

The impact: S&P analysts painted a picture of an improving landscape for public colleges. But disparities exist within the public sector.

Prominent flagship, land-grant and some regional institutions have “maintained or improved their demand metrics,” S&P analysts said in the report. They also pointed to increases in fundraising, state appropriations and investment income that have helped offset inflation for most public colleges.

However, with some exceptions, smaller and more regional public colleges face greater competition and risk.

“Large flagship institutions with demand elasticity, sound resources, and excellent reputations remain well positioned despite emerging credit risks, while regional institutions with weaker demand and less financial flexibility contend with heightened pressures,” analysts said.

Meanwhile, the private nonprofits face numerous enrollment and fiscal challenges. Analysts pointed to “intensifying rivalry for new students” that has led to increasing tuition discounting.

The context: Public colleges’ enrollment growth in fiscal 2025 was a full percentage point higher than the prior year’s 1.1% gain.Before fall 2023, the sector experienced six years of dwindling demand.

Private institutions’ more modest gains still represented an improvement over the 0.4% enrollment growth seen in fiscal 2024, according to S&P. But tuition discounting and rising costs led to worsening operating margins for that group.

By the numbers

21

The number of times S&P downgraded private colleges since June 2025, compared to only three that saw upgrades. Conversely, upgrades exceeded downgrades at public institutions, with nine versus three

3

Years in a row that median operating margins have been negative for private colleges, according to S&P

79.4%

The median share of revenue generated from students at private nonprofits, according to S&P. The figure represents a diversification of revenue compared to the 84% share in 2020

title: MacKenzie Scott once couldn’t afford dentist, now gives $20M to struggling teens
summary: Philanthropist MacKenzie Scott gave a record $20 million to Active Minds. This donation addresses the critical youth mental health crisis in America. Scott's past financial struggles influenced her generous giving approach. The funding will expand mental health programs across schools and universities. Active Minds aims to reduce stigma and improve support accessibility for young people.
full_text:
Jeff Bezos and Mackenzie Scott

Billionaire philanthropist MacKenzie Scott, who once had to fix her own broken tooth with denture glue because she could not afford a dentist, has given a record $20 million donation to a charity working to address the youth mental health crisis in the United States. The donation to the non-profit organization Active Minds is the largest single gift in the charity's history. It comes at a critical time for American teenagers, with data from Fortune showing that nearly one in five adolescents now report having thoughts of self-harm. Scott's donation is enormous compared to the charity's usual finances. Active Minds reported about $9.9 million in annual revenue during the 2025 financial year, meaning this one donation is more than double the amount the organization raised during that year. Now worth an estimated $36 billion according to Forbes, Scott has spent the past seven years giving away an average of almost $10 million every day.

Remembering the weight of poverty before endless fortune

Scott's approach to giving is influenced by the financial struggles she experienced when she was younger. While studying at Princeton University, she managed a demanding academic schedule while also working 30 hours a week doing manual jobs. At one point, she was found crying on campus because she feared she would have to leave university after falling $1,000 short of paying her tuition fees. A friend later arranged a loan that allowed her to complete her degree.

Mackenzie’s Princeton roommate Jeannie Tarkenton loaned her $1000

Her financial hardship also affected her basic healthcare. She once used over-the-counter denture adhesive to hold a broken tooth together because she could not afford treatment. A local dentist later noticed her condition and treated her free of charge. The stress of those difficult years also affected her writing. In a May 1990 letter published in the Princeton Alumni Weekly, Scott thanked her mentor, the famous author Toni Morrison, for giving her "therapy and breathing lessons" while helping her stop worrying so much about revising and finishing her writing.

Driving the early days of Amazon in a borrowed car...

Years after graduating, Scott was still living a modest life as she helped build Amazon with her then-husband, Jeff Bezos. In 1994, Bezos left his high-paying Wall Street job, where he earned the equivalent of $1.5 million to $2 million a year in today's money, to take a chance on the growing internet. Scott fully supported the decision and later said she "couldn't wait to hop in the car." During a five-day trip over the July holiday weekend, the couple drove 2,000 miles across the United States from Texas to Seattle in a borrowed 1988 Chevy Blazer. While Scott drove for most of the journey, Bezos sat in the passenger seat writing the first 30-page draft of Amazon's business plan on his laptop. Using an Excel spreadsheet, he predicted the online bookstore would reach $70 million in sales by 2001. According to journalist Brad Stone, Amazon actually earned more than $3 billion that year. The journey required careful budgeting. When a Motel 6 in Shamrock, Texas, was fully booked, they stayed at a simple roadside motel called the Rambler Motel, where the room was so dirty that Scott refused to remove her shoes. After moving into a garage in Bellevue, Washington, Scott became Amazon's first accountant. She handled the company's bookkeeping, wrote employee paychecks, managed early job interviews, and even negotiated shipping contracts inside a local Barnes and Noble bookstore. Amazon became a public company in 1997 and later grew into a $3 trillion business covering cloud computing, streaming, and artificial intelligence (AI). She got divorced from Bezos in 2019. After that, Scott received a major share of Amazon stock, which she has steadily sold to support charitable causes around the world. She has also faced backlash from billionaires including Tesla CEO Elon Musk for giving away "freebies".

Funding a 'new era' for youth support and mental health

The $20 million grant will help Active Minds expand its mental health programs across hundreds of schools and universities in the United States. The Washington, D.C.-based non-profit currently reaches 4.5 million young people through a network of more than 500 student-led chapters. Active Minds said the funding will help create a "new era of mental health" by making support easier to access in local communities and reducing the stigma around mental health challenges.

Image – Facebook / Active Minds

"This transformational investment allows us to build a future where every young person knows mental health is a vital part of their overall well-being," the organization said. The charity was created after a personal tragedy. Alison Malmon founded Active Minds while she was a junior at the University of Pennsylvania. Her older brother and only sibling, Brian, developed severe depression and psychosis while studying at Columbia University. Brian kept his worsening condition hidden from friends for years before being diagnosed with schizoaffective disorder. He later died by suicide. Malmon started the organization as a small student group to encourage open conversations about mental health. Financial data from the 2024–25 year shows the charity has grown to include 13,485 official chapter members, with student-led events directly reaching more than 400,000 young people with life-saving suicide prevention information.

End of Article

title: Five Things I Wish I Knew My First Semester
summary:

I was making constant small decisions—how to answer student emails, when to grant an extension, what to do when a […]

The post Five Things I Wish I Knew My First Semester appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
My first semester as a faculty member taught me something I wish I had understood on day one: most of the stress did not come from teaching itself. It came from the absence of systems. I was making constant small decisions—how to answer student emails, when to grant an extension, what to do when a student disappeared, how to keep course materials organized, and how to protect research time when the week kept getting fragmented. None of those decisions seemed large in isolation, but together they created a steady drain on time and attention.

What helped was not finding a perfect method. It was building a few repeatable habits that made the semester more manageable for both my students and me. The five practices below are simple, practical, and adaptable across disciplines. They do not eliminate the learning curve of a first semester, but they do reduce unnecessary friction.

1. Create Communication Scripts Before You Need Them

Most student emails fall into a small number of categories: missed work, extension requests, confusion about instructions, grade questions, technology problems, and “I’m behind—what should I do now?” If I wrote every response from scratch, email quickly became a second job. What changed everything was creating a small bank of reusable responses.

A good script has three parts: a respectful acknowledgment, a reference to the relevant course policy or resource, and a next step. For example, instead of writing a long custom reply, I could say, “Thanks for reaching out. Please review the late-work policy in the syllabus, and then submit the assignment by the updated deadline listed in the LMS.” That kind of response is calm, clear, and consistent.

The goal is not to sound robotic. The goal is to reduce decision fatigue and improve fairness. When students receive similar guidance in similar situations, they are less likely to feel that policies are arbitrary. I also learned to send one short weekly announcement in my LMS that answered common questions before students needed to ask them: what is due, what to prioritize, and what usually causes trouble that week. Those announcements prevented many repeat emails before they ever landed in my inbox.

2. Make Expectations Explicit Early

Many first-semester problems are not really performance problems; they are expectation problems. Students often do poorly not because they are unwilling to succeed, but because they are guessing about what “good participation,” “professional communication,” or “acceptable collaboration” actually means.

One of the most useful things I did was create a single “How to succeed in this course” page. I included communication norms, participation expectations, late-work rules, where to find assignments, how quickly I respond to email, and what students should do if they fall behind. I also addressed issues that now matter in almost every class, such as responsible use of AI tools and how to distinguish collaboration from unauthorized help.

The important part is not just posting expectations once. It is revisiting them early and enforcing them gently but consistently. If a student sends an unprofessional email in week two, that is the right time to redirect them. If several students misunderstand an assignment, that is a signal to clarify the directions immediately. Small course corrections early prevent repeated negotiations later. Clear expectations are not about being rigid; they are about making the course more predictable and easier to navigate.

3. Build a Default Weekly Workflow

In a first semester, it is easy to let the calendar decide everything for you. Meetings get scheduled, student needs pop up, grading expands, and research time disappears into whatever space is left. I learned that if I did not build a default week, the week built itself around the most immediate demand.

My solution was simple: protect a few recurring blocks. I designated specific times for course prep, grading, and scholarship. Even a single 60-minute protected block was more effective than hoping I would “find time” later. I also started grading in batches. Instead of checking the LMS constantly and responding to each new submission or question as it appeared, I grouped similar tasks together. That made me faster, more focused, and more consistent in my evaluation of student work.

Another small habit helped more than I expected: I kept a running “next semester fixes” list. When I noticed an unclear instruction, an awkward assignment sequence, or a resource students kept missing, I wrote it down rather than trying to rebuild the course mid-semester. That list lowered my stress because it let me acknowledge a problem without turning it into an emergency. Sometimes the most sustainable move is not to fix everything now, but to capture it for later.

4. Ask for Mid-Semester Feedback While You Can Still Use It

End-of-term evaluations tell us how students felt after the course is over. Mid-semester feedback tells us what we can still improve while the course is in motion. Once I began using a short anonymous check-in, I found it to be one of the most efficient teaching tools I had.

I kept it to five questions: What is helping your learning? What is still unclear? Is the pacing manageable? Is the workload reasonable? What is one change that would help you succeed? Those questions provided useful information without causing survey fatigue. More importantly, they helped me identify friction points that were easy to fix: unclear instructions, too many clustered due dates, or a resource that students did not realize was available.

The real value comes from closing the loop. In the next class or announcement, I would briefly say, “Here is what I heard, here is what I am going to adjust, and here is what will stay the same.” Students responded well when they saw that feedback had a purpose. I did not need to adopt every suggestion. I just needed to show that I was listening and making thoughtful decisions. That transparency improved trust, engagement, and, ultimately, the course’s tone.

5. Learn Your Campus Referral Network Before a Problem Becomes a Crisis

One of the hardest parts of a first semester is realizing how many student issues are not purely instructional in nature. Students may struggle with attendance, accommodations, mental health concerns, financial pressure, technology barriers, conduct issues, or personal crises. New faculty often feel pressure to solve these situations on their own. That is rarely the best approach.

What helped me was learning the referral map early. I needed to know who handled disability accommodations, student conduct, counseling and wellness, academic support, Title IX concerns, library assistance, and LMS or classroom technology problems. I also needed to understand an important professional boundary: my job was not to investigate everything or become the sole support system. My job was to respond appropriately, document when needed, and connect students to the right office.

This is practical workload management as much as it is student support. When faculty know where to refer, they act more consistently and with less uncertainty. Instead of improvising under pressure, they can say, “Here is the office that can help, and here is your next step.” That helps students faster and reduces the isolation many new instructors feel when difficult situations arise.

A Final Thought

If I could go back and advise myself before that first semester began, I would not say, “Work harder.” I would say, “Build better systems sooner.” A few well-designed habits can dramatically reduce the chaos that makes new teaching feel overwhelming.

For anyone starting out, I recommend choosing one practical change this week:

Create three email scripts you know you will reuse.

Post one weekly LMS announcement template.

Draft a five-question mid-semester check-in.

Identify the three campus offices you are most likely to need.

You do not need to solve everything at once. The goal is not perfection. The goal is to build a sustainable way of teaching—one that supports students while also protecting your time, attention, and confidence.

Peter Szawranskyj holds both a bachelor’s and a master’s degree from Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, where his graduate studies focused on safety and human factors. He is currently pursuing a PhD in Occupational Safety and Health at West Virginia University, with a research focus on human factors, training, and safety behavior in aviation. His academic and research interests include advanced cockpit design, cognitive science, and aviation safety systems. He currently serves as a faculty member in the Department of Aeronautical Science at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, where he teaches and mentors future aviation professionals. In addition, he serves as a faculty mentor, supporting and guiding new faculty in their professional development and instructional effectiveness. In this role, he draws on more than three decades of military and civilian aviation experience to bring a practical, safety-focused perspective to the classroom. His instruction emphasizes real-world applications of human factors, crew resource management, flight department operations, and advanced flight systems.

In addition to his academic responsibilities, Peter also serves as the Director of Aviation for a large corporate flight department. In this capacity, he oversees operations for a fleet that includes two Challenger jets and is actively involved in all aspects of flight department management, including flight operations, regulatory compliance, and safety oversight. His leadership in this role provides valuable, current industry insights that enhance his teaching and benefit his students. Peter began his flying career as an F-14 Tomcat pilot in the United States Navy. Following his service, he held various roles in the airline, charter, and corporate aviation sectors, including Safety Officer, Chief Pilot, and Director of Operations. He holds type ratings in the A320, B737, BE-300, BE-400, CL-30, CL-604, DA-50, G-IV, G-V, and MU-300.

Outside of his professional work, Peter is an avid adventurer. He enjoys scuba diving, hang gliding, and soaring in his Stemme S12 motor glider. He also volunteers with wildlife rehabilitation efforts, helping to care for injured and orphaned animals in his community.
